topic: Testing REQUIRES_NEW commit boundaries with Testcontainers
tomorrowTopic: Transaction boundaries: proxies, propagation and commits

hook.headline: Test the commit boundary, not the annotation
hook.hook: A transaction test is useful only when it proves what remains committed after the surrounding operation actually rolls back.
hook.visualCaption: Run the real service flow, force the outer rollback, then inspect PostgreSQL from outside that transaction.
hook.microExample: outer rollback → audit REQUIRES_NEW commit → row still exists

mentalModel.title: Observe state after rollback
mentalModel.coreIdea: To verify REQUIRES_NEW isolation, exercise the application through its Spring proxies, make the outer transaction fail, then query the database after that call has returned. The assertion should observe committed PostgreSQL state, not state hidden inside a test-managed transaction.
mentalModel.keyOutcome: The test proves the audit commit survives rollback of the surrounding business transaction.
mentalModel.mentalShortcut: invoke → rollback outer → query fresh → verify commit

code.title: Assert after the rollback
code.intro: Keep this test outside Spring's test-managed transaction and inspect committed state after the service fails.
code.highlightReason: The database query runs after the failing service invocation has completed, so it checks externally visible committed state.
code.takeaway: Assert the durable database outcome after the rollback path, rather than merely checking that transactional annotations are present.
code.professionalNote: Use a PostgreSQL Testcontainer when PostgreSQL transaction semantics are part of what the integration test is intended to verify.

production.title: A green test can still prove little
production.scenario: A test expects an audit insert to survive an order rollback. It is annotated @Transactional, calls both repositories directly, and passes without exercising the same boundaries used in production.
problems: A test-managed transaction changes the transactional context in which the application code runs.
Direct repository calls can bypass the service-level proxy and propagation path the test is supposed to verify.
production.professionalApproach: Call the public service entry point without a test-level transaction, deliberately trigger the outer failure, then query the Testcontainers PostgreSQL database and assert the independently committed row remains.
production.debugClue: A test passes when repositories are called directly but fails when the same scenario is executed through the service layer.

interview.question: How would you prove that a Spring REQUIRES_NEW audit write really commits even when the surrounding operation rolls back?
interview.answer: I would write an integration test against PostgreSQL, invoke the real proxied service flow, force the outer transaction to fail, and then query the database after that call completes. I would avoid wrapping the test itself in a test-managed transaction because that changes the surrounding transactional context and can make propagation tests harder to reason about.
